prompt: What is the correct syntax to run onSave() when a button is clicked?
explanation: Event binding wraps the event name in parentheses and runs a template statement: (click)="onSave()".

prompt: What does the $event variable contain for a native DOM event?

options.text: The DOM Event object (with target, target.value, etc.)

explanation: For native events $event is the DOM Event; for custom outputs it's the emitted value.

prompt: Which binding runs submit() only when the Enter key is released in an input?
explanation: The (keyup.enter) key modifier makes Angular filter for the Enter key so you don't inspect event.key by hand.

prompt: What is the difference between [value]="x" and (input)="y($event)"?

options.text: [value] flows data into the element; (input) flows events out to your handler
(input) flows data in; [value] flows events out

explanation: Square brackets are property binding (data in); parentheses are event binding (events out).

prompt: In <input #query (keyup.enter)="search(query.value)" />, what is query?

options.text: A component property declared in the class
A template reference variable that refers to the <input> element
A signal created automatically by Angular

explanation: #query names the element inside the template, so query.value reads what the user typed without any component code.

prompt: Which two properties make computed() efficient?
explanation: A computed signal doesn't run until first read (lazy) and caches its result until a dependency changes (memoized).

prompt: How many times does an effect() run when it is first created?

options.text: At least once, shortly after creation (asynchronously)
Only when read in a template

explanation: Effects are scheduled, not run synchronously: the first run happens during the next change detection, and several changes in a row are batched into one run.

prompt: Copying a value from one signal into another inside an effect() is best replaced by what?
explanation: Deriving state with computed() avoids the ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked errors and extra cycles that state-copying effects cause.

prompt: Which are appropriate use cases for effect()? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Deriving a full name from first and last name signals

explanation: effect() bridges signals to non-reactive APIs; deriving a full name is pure derived state, so it belongs in computed().

prompt: Which function reads a signal's value inside a reactive context WITHOUT registering it as a dependency?
explanation: untracked() lets an effect or computed read a signal without tracking it, avoiding unwanted re-runs.

prompt: Where must effect() be called by default?

options.text: Within an injection context (or pass an explicit Injector)

explanation: effect() needs an injection context so Angular can tie its lifecycle to something; otherwise pass { injector }.

prompt: How do you read the current value of a signal named total?
explanation: A signal is a getter function — call it with parentheses to read its value, both in templates and TypeScript.

prompt: Which methods change the value of a writable signal? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: .set() replaces the value and .update() derives the next value from the current one. There is no .mutate() method.

prompt: Which describes a computed() signal?

options.text: A writable signal you change with .set()
A read-only signal derived from other signals; lazy and memoized
A way to run side effects like logging

explanation: computed() creates a read-only signal that recalculates automatically, only when a dependency changes, and caches its result.

prompt: What is effect() intended for?

options.text: Deriving new state from existing signals
Side effects that reach outside Angular state, like logging or persistence

explanation: Reserve effect() for true side effects; use computed() to keep derived state in sync.

prompt: Which method converts a writable signal into a read-only view for safe exposure from a service?
explanation: Keep the writable signal private and expose this._state.asReadonly() so consumers can read but not overwrite it.

prompt: Why does items().push(item) often fail to update the UI?

options.text: push() is not a valid array method
Signals compare with Object.is, so mutating in place keeps the same reference and detects no change
Arrays cannot be stored in signals

explanation: Because comparison uses Object.is, you must produce a new array, e.g. items.update(curr => [...curr, item]).

prompt: Order these steps to update a counter signal by one.

items.text: Read the current value with count()
The template re-renders with the new value

explanation: Create the signal, read it, update it, and the view reacts automatically.

prompt: Which syntax renders a component value into the page as text?
explanation: Interpolation, {{ value }}, embeds a value into the template as a string.

prompt: Why should you write [disabled]="isSaving()" instead of disabled="{{ isSaving() }}"?

options.text: Interpolation is slower than property binding
Property binding sets the real boolean DOM property; interpolation sets the property to the string "false", which still counts as true
The disabled attribute does not exist on buttons
There is no difference; both work identically

explanation: Interpolation sets disabled to the string "false", and any non-empty string counts as true, so the button never re-enables. Property binding binds a real boolean.

prompt: When must you use attribute binding ([attr.name]) instead of property binding?

options.text: Whenever the value is a string
When the attribute has no matching DOM property, such as colspan or most SVG attributes

explanation: colspan and most SVG attributes have no DOM property, and binding to them directly is a compile error, so use [attr.*]. ARIA attributes can be bound directly since Angular 20, but [attr.aria-*] works in every version.

prompt: Which statements about template expressions are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They are evaluated against the component instance, not global scope
You can reference window, document, and console
Assignments are not allowed (outside event bindings)
You can use the new operator to construct objects

explanation: Template expressions run against the component and forbid globals, new, assignments (outside events), and chained statements.

prompt: What is the modern function that declares a two-way bindable signal input on a custom component (e.g. value = ____<number>(0))?
explanation: model() creates an input that can be read and written and propagates changes back to the parent binding.

prompt: Match each binding syntax to the data-flow direction it represents.
explanation: Interpolation and property binding flow in; event binding flows out; two-way combines both.

prompt: Which expression is required in every @for block?
explanation: track is mandatory in @for — the template won't compile without it. It gives each item a stable identity for efficient DOM reuse.

prompt: Do you need to import CommonModule to use @if, @for, and @switch?

options.text: No — they are built into the template compiler

explanation: Built-in control flow is part of the compiler, so no CommonModule import is needed.

prompt: What operator does @switch use to match a @case, and does it fall through?
explanation: @switch matches with strict === and never falls through, so no break is needed.

prompt: Which contextual variables are available inside an @for block? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: @for exposes $index, $count, $first, $last, $even, and $odd. There is no $key.

prompt: Which optional @for block renders when the collection has zero items?
explanation: @empty gives lists a friendly, intentional empty state.

prompt: When is tracking by $index safe?

options.text: Always — it is the most efficient option
Only for static lists that never reorder or change
Only when the list has unique ids
Never — $index cannot be used for track

explanation: For dynamic lists, track by a stable unique property like id; $index can cause Angular to reuse the wrong DOM nodes.

prompt: A computed() reads showTotal() and, only when it is true, amount(). showTotal is currently false. What happens when amount changes?

options.text: Nothing: amount was not read on the last run, so it is not a dependency

explanation: Dependencies are tracked dynamically: only the signals actually read during the last run count.

prompt: You create selected = linkedSignal(() => sizes()[0]), then call selected.set('Large'). Later sizes is replaced with a new array. What is selected()?

options.text: The first item of the new array, because the source changed
It throws, since linkedSignal is read-only

explanation: A linkedSignal follows its source and accepts manual writes, but a change in the source resets any override.

prompt: Match each signal API to what it gives you.
explanation: linkedSignal() is the hybrid: it derives from a source like computed(), yet you can still call .set() on it.

prompt: With signals, what happens when one signal's value changes?

options.text: Angular re-checks the entire component tree
Only the templates and computations that read that signal are updated
Every effect in the app re-runs

explanation: Reading a signal records a dependency, so a change updates exactly its consumers. That is fine-grained reactivity.

prompt: In a zoneless app, which of these refresh the view? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A signal read by the template changes
Assigning a plain field inside setTimeout

explanation: A plain field assigned in setTimeout, setInterval or subscribe() does not notify Angular. Keep that state in a signal.

prompt: What must you add after a signal named total to read its value in a template, as in {{ total… }}?
explanation: A signal is a function, so calling it, total(), reads the value and registers the dependency.

prompt: What type does computed() return?
explanation: computed() and .asReadonly() both produce a read-only Signal<T> with no .set() or .update().

prompt: When does a callback registered with onCleanup inside an effect run?

options.text: Only once, when the app starts
Before the effect runs again, and when the effect is destroyed
Only when the component is hidden

explanation: Cleanup runs before the next run and on destroy, so timers and listeners from the previous run do not pile up.

prompt: An effect registered a cleanup, and a signal it reads changes. Put the steps in order.

items.text: The effect registers a new cleanup

explanation: The old run is cleaned up first, then the new run starts and registers its own cleanup.

prompt: In a signal state service, how should the writable signal be exposed to components?

options.text: As a public property so components can call .set()
Keep it private; expose .asReadonly() and computed() selectors, and change it through methods
As a plain object copied on every read

explanation: All writes then flow through the service, which is where rules such as "never below zero" are enforced.

prompt: Which binding adds the active class only while isActive() is true?
explanation: [class.name]="flag" toggles a single class and leaves static classes alone.

prompt: Match each goal to its binding syntax.

pairs.left: Set a style with a unit

explanation: Use the object form for several classes and the .unit suffix for styles that need one.

prompt: What does [(ngModel)]="term" combine?

options.text: A property binding in and an event binding out

explanation: The banana in a box is [ ] (value in) wrapped around ( ) (changes out).

prompt: Which module must a standalone component import to use [(ngModel)] on an input?
explanation: Without FormsModule in imports, Angular reports that it cannot bind to ngModel.

prompt: Binding [colspan]="2" on a <td> is a compile error. What should you write instead?
explanation: colspan has no DOM property of that name, so use attribute binding with [attr.colspan].

prompt: With qty = 3, what text does {{ qty() > 2 ? 'many' : 'few' }} render?
explanation: Interpolation evaluates the expression and renders its result as text.

prompt: Which TypeScript type should you give the $event parameter of an (input) handler?
explanation: Type it as Event (or a more specific type) and cast event.target to the element type to read .value.

prompt: Which is the best track expression for a todo list that users can reorder?
explanation: A stable unique id lets Angular keep the right DOM node for each item when the order changes.

prompt: What does @case ('1') do when the switched value is the number 1?

options.text: It matches, because comparison is loose
It does not match, because @switch compares with ===

explanation: @switch uses strict equality, so the string "1" and the number 1 are different values.

prompt: Which keyword saves the value of an @if condition in a variable: @if (user().address; ___ address)?
explanation: The alias lets you reuse the evaluated value inside the block.

prompt: Which command starts the development server with live reload?
explanation: ng serve compiles the app and serves it locally, rebuilding on every change.

prompt: Modern Angular apps default to which component style?
explanation: New CLI projects have been standalone since Angular 17, and since Angular 19 standalone: true is implied, so there is no NgModule boilerplate.

prompt: What language is Angular primarily written in?
explanation: Angular is built with TypeScript, which adds static typing on top of JavaScript.

prompt: What is the difference between ng serve and ng build?

options.text: ng serve runs an in-memory dev server with live reload; ng build writes optimized files to dist/ for deployment
Both produce files you can deploy to production
ng build starts a dev server; ng serve only type-checks
ng serve minifies the app for production; ng build does not

explanation: ng serve is for development only. Deploy the optimized output that ng build writes to dist/.

prompt: Which unit-test runner does a new project created with Angular 21 or later use by default?
explanation: Since Angular 21, new projects run unit tests with Vitest. Existing Karma/Jasmine projects keep working.

prompt: Which CLI command upgrades Angular and runs migrations for breaking changes (ng ____)?
explanation: ng update upgrades packages and runs migration schematics, which is safer than editing package.json by hand.

prompt: Which of these are part of the Angular platform? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Angular ships components, a router, forms and an HTTP client designed to work together. A database is not part of it.

prompt: Where must you run `ng new`?

options.text: Outside any workspace, because it creates one

explanation: ng new creates the workspace, so it runs outside one. Commands like ng serve and ng generate run inside it.

prompt: Which Node.js version should you use with Angular?

options.text: None, Angular does not use Node.js

explanation: Angular requires an active LTS Node.js. Old or odd-numbered versions cause cryptic install and build errors.

prompt: In Angular 20 or later, which class file does `ng generate component greeting` create?
explanation: Since Angular 20 generated files drop the type suffix, so the file is greeting.ts and the class is Greeting.

prompt: Match each command to what it generates.
explanation: ng generate has short forms for each schematic: c, s, d and p.

prompt: Put the steps of an Angular app starting up in order.
explanation: The page loads, main.ts bootstraps the root component with the app config, and the root component renders into <app-root>.

prompt: Where do you register app-wide providers such as the router?
explanation: app.config.ts holds the providers array that main.ts passes to bootstrapApplication.

prompt: Why use `ng update` instead of editing versions in package.json?

options.text: It also runs migrations that rewrite code affected by breaking changes

explanation: ng update upgrades packages and runs schematics that migrate your code, which manual edits skip.

prompt: How should you move a project from Angular 18 to Angular 21?

options.text: Jump straight to 21 in one step
One major version at a time, testing between steps
Delete the project and run ng new

explanation: Each major version has migrations that the next one builds on, so upgrade step by step and test in between.

prompt: Which decorator turns a class into a component?
explanation: @Component links a class to its template, styles, and selector.

prompt: How do you read the value of a signal input declared as name = input<string>()?
explanation: Signal inputs are read-only signals, so you call them to read the current value, in templates and in code.

prompt: How does a child component tell its parent that something happened?

options.text: It changes the value of its input
It declares an output() and calls .emit(value); the parent listens with (eventName)="handler($event)"
It injects the parent component and calls its methods
It writes to a global variable

explanation: Data flows down through inputs and events flow up through outputs, which keeps the data flow predictable.

prompt: What is the modern function for defining a custom event on a component?
explanation: output() is the current recommended API; it replaces the legacy @Output() + EventEmitter pattern.

prompt: After emitting from an output, which method actually sends the value to listeners (e.g. this.rated.____(value))?
explanation: Call .emit(value) on the output to notify whoever is listening in the parent.

prompt: Which function passes data from a parent down to a child component?
explanation: input() declares a read-only property a parent binds data into; events flow back up via output().

prompt: What does model() create?

options.text: An input and output pair bundled for two-way [(binding)]

explanation: model() wires an input and matching output together so a value flows both directions via [(prop)].

prompt: How should two completely unrelated sibling components share state?

options.text: By prop drilling through every ancestor
Through a shared injectable service, typically providedIn: 'root'

explanation: Inputs/outputs only work parent-child; unrelated components inject the same singleton service and react to its signals.

prompt: Why should you avoid mutating an input() value directly inside a child?

options.text: input() is a read-only signal representing parent-owned data; mutating it breaks unidirectional data flow

explanation: Use model() for shared two-way values or emit an output() and let the parent update its own state.

prompt: When is viewChild() the appropriate tool?

options.text: For passing data down to a child
For imperative access to a child instance, like calling .focus() or .reset()

explanation: viewChild() bypasses the input/output contract, so reserve it for genuinely imperative needs.

prompt: Which variant of input() forces the parent to supply a value or fail at compile time (e.g. title = input.____<string>())?
explanation: input.required<T>() fails fast at compile time instead of silently rendering with undefined.

prompt: Which hook is the earliest safe place to read a @ViewChild reference?
explanation: The view isn't created during ngOnInit, so @ViewChild is undefined until ngAfterViewInit runs. (Only a { static: true } query for an element outside @if/@for is available earlier.)

prompt: What condition must be true for ngOnChanges to fire on an input?

options.text: Any property of the bound object is mutated
The bound value's reference changes (a new object/array/primitive)

explanation: ngOnChanges triggers only on a new reference; mutating an existing object in place does not trigger it.

prompt: What is the modern, recommended way to clean up an RxJS subscription tied to a component?

options.text: Pipe through takeUntilDestroyed() (with DestroyRef when outside an injection context)
Use ngDoCheck to check if destroyed

explanation: takeUntilDestroyed() from @angular/core/rxjs-interop auto-completes on destroy, removing the 'forgot to unsubscribe' leak.

prompt: Why should you avoid putting expensive logic in ngDoCheck or ngAfterViewChecked?

options.text: They only run once, so it's wasteful
They run on every change detection cycle, so heavy work can run many times per interaction

explanation: 'Check' hooks fire on every change detection run; expensive work there degrades performance.

prompt: Order these lifecycle hooks in the sequence Angular calls them (for a component with inputs).
explanation: The constructor runs first, then ngOnChanges before ngOnInit, then ngAfterViewInit, and finally ngOnDestroy at teardown.

prompt: Which injectable class (since v16) lets you register a cleanup callback without implementing ngOnDestroy?
explanation: DestroyRef.onDestroy() registers teardown, and it's what takeUntilDestroyed() uses under the hood.

prompt: What element marks where projected content should render inside a component?
explanation: <ng-content> is the compile-time placeholder for projected content (Angular's equivalent of the native <slot>).

prompt: Against which component's class do bindings inside projected content resolve?

options.text: The parent component that supplies the content
Whichever is closest in the DOM

explanation: Projected content is compiled against the parent's class even though it renders inside the child's DOM.

prompt: With multiple select-based slots and no catch-all, what happens to an element that matches no selector?

options.text: It renders in the first slot
It is silently dropped and not rendered
It renders after the last slot

explanation: Without a plain <ng-content> catch-all, unmatched elements silently disappear from the DOM.

prompt: What is ngProjectAs used for?

options.text: To alias an element's selector identity so it matches a slot (e.g. when wrapped in <ng-container>)

explanation: ngProjectAs takes a static string and tells Angular to treat the element as if it matched that selector.

prompt: Which is the modern, signal-based way to query projected content (stable since v19)?
explanation: contentChild()/contentChildren() return signals; view queries (viewChild) only see the component's own template.

prompt: Why shouldn't you wrap <ng-content> in @if inside the child's own template?

options.text: Angular still creates the projected DOM nodes regardless, so it doesn't give true conditional rendering — use [hidden] or omit the slot instead
@if cannot be used in child components

explanation: Conditionally wrapping <ng-content> doesn't lazily create content; prefer a CSS toggle like [hidden] or fallback content.

prompt:
A parent projects @if (canDelete()) {
…
} into a modal whose footer slot has fallback content. What shows when canDelete() is false?

options.text: Nothing: the footer slot is empty
Both the fallback and the projected content

explanation: Fallback is decided once, when the slot is created, and only appears if nothing at all is projected. The @if block counts as projected content even when false. Put the @if inside an always-projected element instead.

prompt: Match each API to its job in a presentational component.

pairs.right: Data the component can't work without
Reports a user action to the parent
Re-checks only when inputs, events, or read signals change

explanation: Presentational components take essential data through required inputs, report intents through outputs, derive display values with computed(), and use OnPush for cheap change detection.

prompt: An EntryItem has a '+1 rep' button. What should its click handler do?

options.text: Inject the diary service and save the new value
Emit a new object like { ...entry, reps: entry.reps + 1 } and let the parent apply it
Call the parent component directly through viewChild()

explanation: The entry belongs to the parent. The child describes the change with an output, and the owner updates its state immutably.

prompt: Why might this fail to update the view: entries.update(list => { list.push(x); return list; })?

options.text: update() only works with primitive values
It returns the same array reference, so the signal sees no change
push() is not allowed in TypeScript strict mode

explanation: Signals compare values with Object.is. Returning the same reference looks like 'no change'. Return a new array such as [...list, x].

prompt: Put the steps of unidirectional data flow in order, starting from a user clicking Delete.

items.text: The presentational item emits remove with the entry id
The presentational list re-emits the event
The smart page calls the service and filters its entries signal into a new array
The new array flows back down through inputs and the view updates

explanation: Events travel up to the single owner of the state, which updates it, and the new state flows back down.

prompt: Which are signs you should move state into a shared service instead of bubbling events? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Inputs pass through several components that don't use them
Unrelated parts of the page need the same state
A parent and its direct child share one value
You re-emit the same output through four or five layers

explanation: Prop drilling and state shared by unrelated components call for a service. A direct parent-child relationship is exactly what inputs and outputs are for.

prompt: In a unit test, which method on fixture.componentRef sets a signal input?
explanation: fixture.componentRef.setInput('entries', value) sets the input, then fixture.detectChanges() renders it.

prompt: By default, a component's CSS applies to which elements?

options.text: Only the elements in that component's own template
Every element in the whole app

explanation: Angular scopes component styles to the component's own template by default (emulated view encapsulation), so styles do not leak.

prompt: Which CSS selector styles a component's own host element?
explanation: :host targets the element the component is attached to, such as <app-hello-box>. It is inline by default, so :host { display: block } is a common first rule.

prompt: A template contains <app-greeting />, but nothing renders. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Greeting is missing from the imports of the component using it
The selector must start with ng-

explanation: Standalone components must list the components, directives and pipes their template uses in imports.

prompt: Why should input-dependent setup go in ngOnInit rather than the constructor?

options.text: Inputs are set after the class is created, so they are not available in the constructor

explanation: Angular creates the component, then binds inputs, then calls ngOnInit. The constructor is for injection and simple field defaults.

prompt: Does ngOnChanges run when a signal input() receives a new value?

options.text: No, use computed() or effect() with signal inputs instead

explanation: Signal inputs do not trigger ngOnChanges. Derive values with computed() and run side effects with effect().

prompt: When does the callback passed to afterNextRender() run?

options.text: Once, after the next render, and only in the browser
Before every render, on the server too

explanation: afterNextRender() runs once after rendering and never during server-side rendering, which makes it safe for DOM APIs.

prompt: Which of these keep running after a component is destroyed unless you stop them? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A window event listener added by hand
A single HTTP request that has already completed

explanation: Timers, endless streams and manual listeners outlive the component. An HTTP request completes on its own and needs no cleanup.

prompt: What does a viewChild() signal hold before the element has been rendered?
explanation: The view is built after the class, so an optional query is undefined until the element exists. viewChild.required throws if read too early.

prompt: Match each query to what it searches.

pairs.right: Content projected in by a parent

explanation: View queries look at your own template. Content queries look at what a parent placed between your tags.

prompt: What does a pipe do to the underlying data it transforms?

options.text: It permanently converts the stored value
It leaves the data unchanged and only changes how it is displayed
It deletes the original and replaces it
It moves the value into a signal

explanation: A pipe transforms a value for display via the | operator without modifying the underlying data.

prompt: In a standalone component, what must you do before using CurrencyPipe in the template?

options.text: Nothing — built-in pipes are always available
Import it and add it to the component's imports array

explanation: Standalone components must import each pipe by name, e.g. imports: [CurrencyPipe]; otherwise you get 'No pipe found'.

prompt: Why is the async pipe recommended for displaying Observables?

options.text: It subscribes, shows the latest value, and unsubscribes automatically when the component is destroyed
It converts the Observable into a signal

explanation: The async pipe manages the whole subscription lifecycle, preventing memory leaks and removing manual subscribe/unsubscribe code.

prompt: Which of the following built-in pipes are impure (re-run on every change detection cycle)? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: async, json, slice, and keyvalue are impure by design. uppercase is a pure pipe.

prompt: Which character passes an argument to a pipe, as in date____'short'?
explanation: A colon separates each pipe argument, e.g. {{ today | date:'short' }} or currency:'USD':'symbol':'1.2-2'.

prompt: Why should you avoid writing data$ | async more than once for the same Observable?

options.text: Each occurrence creates a new subscription (and possibly a new HTTP request)
The async pipe can only be used once per template

explanation: Subscribe once with @if (data$ | async; as data) and reuse the alias to avoid duplicate subscriptions.

prompt: What is the difference between an attribute directive and a structural directive?

options.text: Attribute directives have templates; structural directives do not
An attribute directive changes its host element; a structural directive adds or removes views from a template
Structural directives can only be used on <div> elements
There is no difference; the names are interchangeable

explanation: Attribute directives change the look or behavior of their host element. Structural directives (used with *) create and remove views from an <ng-template>.

prompt: Which selector makes a directive apply to any element with an appHighlight attribute?
explanation: Square brackets make it an attribute selector. 'appHighlight' without brackets would match an <appHighlight> element.

prompt: Which @Directive property declares bindings and event listeners on the host element, e.g. { "(mouseenter)": "active.set(true)" }?
explanation: The host property is the recommended replacement for the @HostBinding and @HostListener decorators.

prompt: Match each API to its role in a structural directive.

pairs.right: The template the directive sits on

explanation: A structural directive renders its TemplateRef into its ViewContainerRef, and clears it when the content should disappear.

prompt: A component lists { directive: ClickOutside } in hostDirectives. Can its users write (appClickOutside)="close()"?

options.text: Yes, all host directive inputs and outputs are public
No, unless the output is listed in the entry's outputs array (optionally with an alias)
Only if the component also imports ClickOutside
No, host directives cannot have outputs

explanation: A host directive's inputs and outputs are private unless you expose them, e.g. outputs: ['appClickOutside: dismissed'].

prompt: Why should a structural directive avoid calling clear() and createEmbeddedView() on every change?

options.text: It is not allowed inside effect()
Rebuilding destroys and recreates the content, losing focus and component state
createEmbeddedView() can only be called once per app

explanation: Track whether the view exists, create it once when needed, and clear it once when it should go away.

prompt: Which interface does a custom pipe class implement?
explanation: A custom pipe is a class decorated with @Pipe that implements PipeTransform and its transform() method.

prompt: How do you format a date inside a component's TypeScript, where the | operator is unavailable?

options.text: Pipes cannot be reproduced in code

explanation: formatDate, formatCurrency, formatNumber and formatPercent do in code what the pipes do in templates. Pass the locale from inject(LOCALE_ID).

prompt: What do you need so the date and currency pipes format for German users?

options.text: registerLocaleData(localeDe) and a LOCALE_ID provider set to 'de'
Nothing, pipes detect the browser language on their own
A custom pipe for every format

explanation: Pipes default to en-US. Register the locale data and provide LOCALE_ID so every formatting pipe follows it.

prompt: Which built-in pipe lets you loop over the entries of an object?
explanation: keyvalue turns an object into an array of { key, value } pairs that @for can iterate.

prompt: An attribute directive does nothing and the console shows no error. What should you check first?

options.text: That the directive is in the component's imports
That the CLI is up to date

explanation: An unknown attribute is valid HTML, so Angular ignores it silently. A missing import is the most common cause, followed by a selector without brackets.

prompt: What is the recommended way for a directive to toggle a class on its host element?

options.text: An entry in the host property, such as '[class.active]': 'active()'

explanation: The host property is declarative, works with server-side rendering and keeps all host behavior in one place. @HostBinding still works but is no longer the recommended style.

prompt: Why does a pure pipe not update after you call items.push(x) on the array it receives?

options.text: The array reference is the same, so the pure pipe does not re-run
push() is not allowed in Angular
Pure pipes only run once per component

explanation: Pure pipes re-run when the input reference changes. Replace the array with a new one to trigger them.

prompt: In {{ today | date:'fullDate' | uppercase }}, which pipe runs first?

options.text: They run at the same time

explanation: Chained pipes apply left to right, so date formats the value and uppercase then changes its case.

prompt: What is the recommended way to register a service as an app-wide, tree-shakable singleton?

options.text: Add it to every component's providers array
Declare it in an NgModule's declarations

explanation: providedIn: 'root' gives one shared instance app-wide and lets the bundler drop it if never injected.

prompt: What happens if you add a service that is already providedIn: 'root' to a component's own providers array?

options.text: Nothing changes; it stays a global singleton
That component and its children get their own separate instance

explanation: A component-level provider creates a new scoped instance for that subtree, which can silently break singleton state sharing.

prompt: Why does calling inject() inside a setTimeout callback throw an error?

options.text: inject() only works in constructors literally
inject() must run synchronously within a valid injection context, which is gone once the async callback fires
You can only inject one dependency per callback

explanation: Capture the dependency in a field during construction, then use it later inside the callback.

prompt: When should you use an InjectionToken instead of a class for a dependency?

options.text: When the dependency is not a class — e.g. config objects, primitives, functions, or browser APIs

explanation: InjectionToken gives type-safe DI for non-class values and avoids the collisions of raw string tokens.

prompt: Match each provider recipe to what it does.

pairs.right: Call a function to compute the value

explanation: These four recipes are the mechanism behind swapping implementations and mocking in tests.

prompt: Which modern function is the recommended way to retrieve a dependency, usable in guards, resolvers, and effect() as well as constructors?
explanation: inject() works as a field initializer and in any valid injection context, not just constructors.

prompt: ThemeService is providedIn: 'root' and injects FEATURE_FLAGS. A component overrides FEATURE_FLAGS in its own providers and injects ThemeService. Which FEATURE_FLAGS value does ThemeService see?

options.text: The component's override, because the component asked for ThemeService
The root value, unless ThemeService is also provided in that component
Neither: Angular throws a provider conflict error

explanation: A service resolves its dependencies from the injector that created it. The root ThemeService was created by the root injector, so it reads the root value. Provide ThemeService in the component too if it must see the override.

prompt: CartService is providedIn: 'root'. A product page also lists it in its component providers. What happens?

options.text: Nothing changes; Angular reuses the root instance
The product page and its children get a second, separate instance, so the rest of the app doesn't see their changes
Angular throws a duplicate provider error
The root instance is destroyed and replaced

explanation: Each injector caches its own instance. A component-level provider creates a new instance for that subtree, which breaks sharing with the rest of the app.

prompt: Match each provider location to what it gives you.

pairs.right: One instance for the whole app
One instance shared by a feature's route subtree
A private instance per component, shared with its children

explanation: Use root for shared state, route providers to scope state to one feature, and component providers for state that must be private to one widget.

prompt: Which belong in a facade's public API? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Read-only computed() selectors like entries and loading
Intent methods like add() and remove(id)
The injected HttpClient so components can make their own calls

explanation: Components should read state through read-only selectors and change it only through intent methods. Writable state and HttpClient stay hidden.

prompt: Order the steps of an optimistic delete inside a facade.

items.text: Remember the entry and its position
Patch state with a new array that leaves the entry out
Call the API to delete it
If the call fails, put the entry back and set an error message

explanation: Save what you need to undo, update the UI immediately, call the server, and roll back on failure.

prompt: Why split a feature into an API service and a facade?

options.text: Angular requires HttpClient to be injected in a separate class
The API service knows endpoints and mapping; the facade knows state and rules, so each stays small and testable

explanation: Separating HTTP from state lets you test the facade with a stubbed API and change endpoints without touching state logic.

prompt: Which signal method returns a read-only view of a writable signal, so other classes can read it but not set it?
explanation: Keep the writable signal private and expose signal.asReadonly() or a computed() selector.

prompt: When a component asks for a dependency, where does Angular look first?

options.text: The component's own element injector, then its parents up to the root

explanation: Angular walks up the injector tree from the asking component until it finds a provider.

prompt: Where can you safely call inject()?
explanation: Field initializers, constructors and factory functions run in an injection context. Lifecycle hooks and async callbacks do not.

prompt: Each editor widget on a page should have its own private state. Where do you provide the state service?
explanation: A component's providers create one instance per component instance, destroyed with the component.

prompt: What does inject(Logger, { optional: true }) return when nothing provides Logger?
explanation: With optional: true the lookup returns null instead of throwing a No provider error.

prompt: Which of these leak a facade's internals? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A public writable signal that components can .set()
Exposing a raw http$ Observable for components to subscribe to

explanation: Writable signals, HTTP-verb names and raw response streams hand the internals back to components. A computed selector is read-only and fine.

prompt: What does providedIn: 'root' give a service?

options.text: One shared instance, dropped from the bundle if nothing injects it
A new instance for every component
An instance only for lazy routes
No instance until it is added to providers

explanation: providedIn: 'root' makes an app-wide, tree-shakable singleton with no providers entry needed.

prompt: When is an optimistic update a poor fit?

options.text: A payment, where the confirmed result matters before the user continues

explanation: Optimistic updates suit quick, reversible actions that usually succeed. Where confirmation matters, wait for the server.

prompt: Why use routerLink instead of href for links inside the app?

options.text: href does not work in Angular templates
routerLink navigates on the client without reloading the page
routerLink makes links open in a new tab

explanation: A plain href triggers a full page reload. routerLink lets the Router swap the page component inside <router-outlet />.

prompt: Which provideRouter feature binds a route parameter like :id to a matching component input? provideRouter(routes, ____())
explanation: withComponentInputBinding() passes route params (and query params and resolved data) into inputs with the same name.

prompt: Which statements about loadComponent in a route are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It downloads the page's code the first time the route is visited
It requires the page to be declared in an NgModule
It keeps the initial bundle smaller

explanation: loadComponent lazy-loads a standalone component, so its code is only downloaded when the user first navigates there.

prompt: How is a route parameter declared in a route's path?
explanation: A colon prefix (:id) marks a dynamic segment that matches any value in that URL position.

prompt: What must you enable to bind route params directly to component inputs?
explanation: withComponentInputBinding() maps route/query params onto matching component inputs automatically.

prompt: Why can reading a param only in ngOnInit() via snapshot cause stale-data bugs?

options.text: Angular reuses the same component instance when navigating between sibling routes, so ngOnInit doesn't re-run
snapshot only works with query params
ngOnInit runs before the router is ready

explanation: On /products/1 → /products/2 the component is reused; use paramMap observable, toSignal, or input binding to react.

prompt: What is the key difference between a route parameter and a query parameter?

options.text: Route params are optional; query params are required
A route param identifies which resource you're viewing; a query param carries optional context like sort or page
Query params always appear before the path

explanation: If removing the value means a different thing, it's a route param; if it just changes how the same thing displays, it's a query param.

prompt: Route parameters are always delivered to your code as what type?
explanation: Params are always strings; use a transform like numberAttribute or Number() to convert, e.g. for numeric ids.

prompt: When a param change should trigger a new HTTP request, which RxJS operator cancels the previous in-flight request?
explanation: switchMap re-triggers the request on each paramMap emission and cancels stale requests to avoid race conditions.

prompt: What is the difference between canActivate and canMatch returning false?

options.text: canActivate blocks navigation; canMatch tells the router to try the next route definition with the same path

explanation: canMatch's false means 'not a match here, try the next config' — ideal for feature flags and A/B testing.

prompt: How should a functional guard redirect a user?
explanation: Returning a UrlTree/RedirectCommand is the value the router is built around; navigate()+false can race with the router.

prompt: What does a resolver do?

options.text: Fetches data before a route finishes activating, so the component has it on first render

explanation: A ResolveFn pre-fetches data; the router waits for it before activation, avoiding empty-then-spinner flicker.

prompt: How can a component receive resolved data without injecting ActivatedRoute?

options.text: Enable withComponentInputBinding() and declare an input matching the resolve key

explanation: withComponentInputBinding() flows resolved data (and route/query params) into matching input()/input.required() properties.

prompt: Why shouldn't client-side route guards be treated as a complete security solution?

options.text: They only run on the server
Guard code runs in the user's browser and can be inspected or modified, so the server must enforce authorization too

explanation: Guards improve UX and cut unnecessary requests, but authorization must be independently enforced on the server.

prompt: Order these navigation-lifecycle steps as the router evaluates them.
explanation: The router runs canMatch while matching, then canDeactivate for the route being left, then canActivateChild/canActivate for the new route, then resolvers, and finally activates the component.

prompt: Why should the wildcard route { path: '**' } be the last entry in a routes array?

options.text: Routes are matched top to bottom, and ** matches everything, so later routes would never be reached
Angular sorts routes alphabetically and ** sorts last
It is only valid at the end of the file
Lazy routes cannot be declared after it

explanation: The first matching route wins. A wildcard placed early swallows every URL after it.

prompt: Navigation seems to do nothing: the URL changes but the page content never updates. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: There is no <router-outlet /> where the matched component can render
The routes array has too many entries

explanation: The router matches the route, but a page needs an outlet to render into.

prompt: You change the sort order with router.navigate([], { queryParams: { sort: 'price' } }) and the active ?page=3 disappears. How do you keep the other query parameters?
explanation: By default a navigation replaces the whole query string. 'merge' keeps existing keys and overrides only the ones you pass.

prompt: A parent route with children matches, but the child component never appears. What is missing?

options.text: A nested <router-outlet /> in the parent component's template
A canActivate guard on the child

explanation: Each nesting level needs its own outlet. The parent's outlet is where its matched child renders.

prompt: What does a canDeactivate guard receive as its first argument?

options.text: The component instance that is about to be left
The URL the user is going to

explanation: canDeactivate gets the component being destroyed, so it can check that component's own state such as a dirty form.

prompt: Which situations are NOT covered by a canDeactivate guard? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Clicking a routerLink to another page
Typing a new address into the address bar

explanation: The router only sees navigations inside the app. Tab close, reload and typed addresses need a beforeunload handler.

prompt: In a guard factory such as roleGuard(role): CanActivateFn, where must inject() be called?

options.text: Inside the returned guard function, which runs in an injection context
In the outer factory function, when the route table is built

explanation: The factory runs when routes are defined, outside any injection context. The returned guard runs per navigation, where inject() is allowed.

prompt: A resolver's HTTP call returns 404 and nothing handles the error. What does the user experience?

options.text: The navigation fails and they stay on the previous page with no message
The page renders with empty data
They are redirected to the wildcard route automatically
The error is retried three times

explanation: An erroring resolver cancels navigation (NavigationError). Handle it with catchError and return a RedirectCommand.

prompt: A lazy-loaded admin route is protected only by canActivate. What happens to visitors who are not admins?

options.text: The admin chunk is still downloaded before the guard turns them away
The route is removed from the bundle
The guard runs before the router matches the path

explanation: canActivate runs after matching, so the chunk has already loaded. Use canMatch to skip the route and its download.

prompt: Which URL design follows the rule 'identity in the path, view state in the query'?
explanation: 42 identifies which product, so it is a route parameter. Sorting and paging only change how things are shown, so they are query parameters.

prompt: Which module must you import to use ngModel, ngForm, and ngModelGroup?
explanation: Template-driven form directives come from FormsModule; add it to the standalone component's imports array.

prompt: Why is the name attribute required on an ngModel input inside a <form>?

options.text: Angular uses it as the key to register the control within the form's FormGroup
It is only needed for styling

explanation: Without name (and without standalone options), Angular can't register the control and throws a runtime error.

prompt: The [(ngModel)] "banana in a box" syntax is shorthand for which combination?
explanation: [(ngModel)]="x" expands to [ngModel]="x" (ngModelChange)="x = $event" — property binding in, event binding out.

prompt: When should validation error messages be shown for the best UX?

options.text: Only after the field is touched and/or dirty
Only after the form is submitted successfully
Never — rely on the disabled button

explanation: Gating messages behind touched/dirty avoids scolding users before they've interacted with the field.

prompt: Which directive groups related controls into a nested FormGroup (e.g. an address block)?
explanation: ngModelGroup="address" produces a nested form value like { address: { street, city } } that mirrors your data model.

prompt: Even with [disabled]="form.invalid" on the submit button, why should onSubmit re-check form.invalid?

options.text: A disabled button can be bypassed, so it is not real validation/security

explanation: Disabling the button is only UX; always re-validate in the handler (and on the server).

prompt: What is the core difference between reactive and template-driven forms?

options.text: In reactive forms the form model is defined explicitly in the component class and is the source of truth

explanation: Reactive forms build an explicit FormControl/FormGroup/FormArray tree in TypeScript, giving synchronous access and testability.

prompt: What must a synchronous custom validator return?

options.text: true if valid, false if invalid
null if valid, or a ValidationErrors object describing what failed

explanation: A ValidatorFn returns null when valid or an errors object like { passwordMismatch: true } when invalid.

prompt: Where should a validator that compares password and confirmPassword be attached?

options.text: On the FormGroup that contains both fields

explanation: Cross-field validators need both sibling values, so they live on the containing FormGroup.

prompt: What's the difference between form.value and form.getRawValue()?

options.text: form.value excludes disabled controls; getRawValue() includes every control's value

explanation: Disabled controls are silently omitted from form.value; use getRawValue() when you need them all.

prompt: Which control type handles a dynamic, repeatable list where the number of controls isn't known ahead of time?
explanation: FormArray indexes controls by position, ideal for user-added items like a list of skills or phone numbers.

prompt: In a submit handler, which method forces validation messages to appear when a user submits without touching any field (form.____())?
explanation: markAllAsTouched() reveals touched-gated error messages even when the user never focused a field.

prompt: What must a synchronous ValidatorFn return?

options.text: null when valid, or a ValidationErrors object when invalid

explanation: A ValidatorFn is (control) => ValidationErrors | null; null means valid, an errors object describes what failed.

prompt: Why must an async validator's Observable complete?

options.text: Otherwise it uses too much memory
Angular waits for completion to move the control out of PENDING; a non-completing stream leaves it pending forever

explanation: Use first() or take(1) (or rely on HttpClient completing) so the control can resolve to VALID/INVALID.

prompt: What is a validator factory?

options.text: A service that stores all validators
A function that returns a ValidatorFn/AsyncValidatorFn, so the rule can be parameterized and reused

explanation: Factories like minAgeValidator(18) return a configured validator, keeping rules reusable across the app.

prompt: While an async validator is running, what is the control's status?
explanation: PENDING means 'I don't know yet' — neither valid nor invalid — so the UI can show a 'checking…' state.

prompt: Which techniques keep an async validator that checks the server while the user types efficient and resilient? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Start the request from timer(400) so quick typing never reaches the server
switchMap from the timer to the HTTP request
catchError so a failed check does not block the form

explanation: Angular unsubscribes from the previous validation on every value change, so a short timer acts as a debounce and switchMap starts the request. distinctUntilChanged has no effect inside a validator, because each call creates a stream with a single value.

prompt: Where should a validator that compares two sibling fields be attached?

options.text: On one of the individual FormControls
On the parent FormGroup (or FormArray), which can read both via group.get()

explanation: A single control can't read its siblings; cross-field checks belong on the group that contains them.

prompt: What is the primary purpose of ControlValueAccessor?

options.text: To bridge Angular's forms API and a custom component's UI so it behaves like a native control

explanation: CVA lets any component work with formControlName/[formControl]/ngModel by syncing value, touched, and disabled state.

prompt: Which CVA method handles the model → view direction (e.g. setValue, patchValue, reset)?
explanation: writeValue updates the component's internal state when the FormControl's value changes programmatically.

prompt: Why does the NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR provider need forwardRef(() => MyComponent)?

options.text: Because the provider is part of the class's own decorator metadata, which may be evaluated before the class is fully defined
It is optional and never needed

explanation: forwardRef defers resolving the self-reference until Angular actually needs it, so it is the always-safe form.

prompt: What happens if you forget multi: true on the NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR provider?

options.text: The forms directive no longer receives a list of accessors, and you get a runtime error instead of a working control
The component throws a compile error

explanation: NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR is a multi-provider token: the forms directive expects a list of accessors, which multi: true provides.

prompt: Does ControlValueAccessor perform validation?

options.text: No — it only syncs value, touched, and disabled; validation uses Validators or the Validator/NG_VALIDATORS interface

explanation: Value synchronization and validation are intentionally separate concerns with separate tokens.

prompt: Match each ControlValueAccessor method to its role.

pairs.right: Model → view: update UI from the FormControl
Store the callback to call on user value changes
Store the callback to call on blur/touch

explanation: Together these four methods implement the full contract Angular's forms directives expect.

prompt: A custom control injects NgControl with { self: true } and also provides NG_VALIDATORS pointing to itself. What happens when it is used with formControlName?

options.text: The value accessor is registered twice

explanation: formControlName asks the element for NG_VALIDATORS, which points back at the component while the component is still waiting for NgControl. A self-validating control should register both NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR and NG_VALIDATORS as providers instead.

prompt: A control uses updateOn: 'blur'. While the user is typing, what does control.value contain?

options.text: The old value; it updates when the field loses focus
null until the form is submitted

explanation: updateOn delays when the value is committed to the control, not just when messages show, so the value stays at its previous content until blur.

prompt: You call control.setValue('x') from code. Which statement is true afterwards?

options.text: The control is still pristine, because only user edits make it dirty
The control is dirty and touched
The control is touched but pristine

explanation: dirty means the user changed the value. Programmatic setValue does not mark the control dirty or touched.

prompt: Why is tracking a FormArray's @for list by the control object safer than track $index when items can be removed from the middle?

options.text: After a removal the later items shift index, so $index reuses the DOM of the wrong row
Controls are faster to compare than numbers

explanation: With track $index, deleting item 1 makes item 2 become index 1, so Angular reuses the wrong row's DOM and focus. Tracking the control keeps identity stable.

prompt: A reactive form's inputs lose what the user typed after every keystroke. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The FormGroup is built inside a getter or method that runs on every change detection

explanation: A getter that builds a new group returns fresh, empty controls on each call. Build the form once as a field or in the constructor.

prompt: What is the recommended way to end a valueChanges subscription created in a component's constructor?

options.text: Do nothing; controls clean up themselves

explanation: valueChanges belongs to the control, which can outlive the view. takeUntilDestroyed() completes the subscription when the component is destroyed.

prompt: A custom control keeps working after form.disable() is called on its FormControl. Which method is missing?
explanation: Angular calls setDisabledState when disable() or enable() is used. Without it the widget stays interactive.

prompt: What must you add before a service can inject HttpClient?
explanation: Register HttpClient once, usually in app.config.ts. Without it you get "No provider for HttpClient".

prompt: When does this.http.get("/api/products") send the request?

options.text: When something subscribes to the returned observable

explanation: HTTP observables are cold: each subscription (subscribe, async pipe, toSignal) sends its own request.

prompt: What does an HttpErrorResponse with status 0 usually mean?

options.text: The request succeeded with an empty body
No response arrived: offline, server unreachable, or blocked by CORS
The JSON could not be parsed

explanation: Status 0 means the browser never got an HTTP response. Check the connection and the console for CORS errors.

prompt: What is the safest way to send ?q=rope&page=2 with a GET request?
explanation: The params option builds and encodes the query string for you.

prompt: Which signal-based API loads data over HTTP and re-fetches automatically when signals in its URL function change (____(() => url))?
explanation: httpResource() exposes value(), isLoading(), error(), and reload(). It is stable since Angular 22.

prompt: Your app on localhost:4200 cannot read responses from an API on localhost:3000 because of CORS. What is the usual fix during development?

options.text: Use the dev-server proxy (proxy.conf.json) so the app calls /api on its own origin

explanation: CORS is enforced by the browser and allowed by the server. Locally, ng serve can forward /api calls; in production, configure the server.

prompt: With withInterceptors([a, b]), put the steps of one request and its response in order.
explanation: Requests flow through the array in order, and responses flow back in reverse.

prompt: How should an interceptor add an Authorization header?

options.text: Store the header in localStorage so the browser sends it

explanation: HttpRequest is immutable. headers.set() returns a new HttpHeaders object without changing the request, so you must clone the request.

prompt: Two requests run in parallel. A loading interceptor sets a boolean to true on start and false in finalize. What goes wrong?

options.text: Nothing; finalize waits for all requests
The loader hides when the first request finishes, while the second is still running

explanation: Each request finishes independently. Count pending requests and show the loader while the count is above zero.

prompt: Which class creates a typed key for per-request options that interceptors read with req.context.get()?
explanation: new HttpContextToken<boolean>(() => false) defines an option with a default. Callers set it with new HttpContext().set(TOKEN, true).

prompt: Which are good rules for a retry interceptor? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Retry GET requests on network errors (status 0) or 5xx responses
Retry every POST up to three times
Give up immediately on 4xx errors like 400 or 404
Wait a little longer before each new attempt

explanation: Retry only idempotent requests and only transient failures, with backoff. Retrying POST can create duplicates, and 4xx errors won't fix themselves.

prompt: Why should an auth interceptor check the request's host before attaching the token?

options.text: Angular rejects headers on absolute URLs
To avoid leaking the user's token to third-party APIs and CDNs
Because tokens only work on GET requests

explanation: Interceptors see every HttpClient call, including ones to other hosts. Only your own API should receive the token.

prompt: You want to change only a product's price without resending the whole record. Which method fits best?
explanation: patch sends only the changed fields, while put replaces the whole resource.

prompt: What happens when the function passed to httpResource() returns undefined?

options.text: A request is sent to the URL 'undefined'

explanation: Returning undefined tells httpResource to wait, which is useful while a required input is not available yet.

prompt: Why map server DTOs into your own model inside the data service?

options.text: Components then depend on your shape, and a renamed server field is fixed in one place
It removes the need for types

explanation: Mapping at the boundary isolates the app from backend changes and keeps components free of server details.

prompt: An error-toast interceptor is placed OUTSIDE (before) a retry interceptor. What is the effect?

options.text: It only sees the error that remains after all retries
It fires on every failed attempt

explanation: An outer interceptor sees the final result of everything inside it, so it only reports the error that survived the retries. Placed inside the retry, it would fire per attempt.

prompt: What does HttpTestingController.verify() in afterEach guarantee?

options.text: No request was made that the test did not match and answer

explanation: verify() fails if any outstanding request was never matched, so unnoticed extra requests cannot slip through.

prompt: What is a key difference between a Promise and an Observable?

options.text: Promises can emit many values; Observables emit exactly one
An Observable is lazy, can emit many values over time, and is cancellable via unsubscribe()
Promises support operators like map and filter

explanation: A Promise is eager and single-value; an Observable is lazy (runs on subscribe), multi-value, and cancellable.

prompt: What does the async pipe do in a template?

options.text: Converts an Observable into a Promise
Subscribes, shows the latest value, and unsubscribes automatically when the component is destroyed
Runs the Observable only once and caches it forever
Adds error handling to the stream

explanation: The async pipe manages the subscription lifecycle for you, preventing leaks and removing manual subscribe/unsubscribe.

prompt: Which operator cancels a previous in-flight HTTP request when a new search term arrives?
explanation: switchMap cancels the previous inner Observable and switches to the newest — ideal for typeahead search.

prompt: Match each flattening operator to its behavior.

pairs.right: Cancel the old, use the new
Run in order, one at a time

explanation: Choosing the right flattening operator prevents race conditions and duplicate submissions.

prompt: For a manual subscription in component logic, what's the modern way to avoid a memory leak without ngOnDestroy boilerplate?
explanation: takeUntilDestroyed() ties the subscription to the component's DestroyRef and completes it on destroy.

prompt: By convention, variable names holding Observables are suffixed with which single character (e.g. user__)?
explanation: The $ suffix (user$, results$) is a widely adopted convention that makes Observables easy to spot.

prompt: You call takeUntilDestroyed() with no argument inside ngOnInit(). What happens?

options.text: It works, because the component uses inject()
It throws: ngOnInit is not an injection context, so pass a DestroyRef injected in a field

explanation: Without an argument, takeUntilDestroyed() injects DestroyRef itself, which only works in a constructor or field initializer. In ngOnInit, use takeUntilDestroyed(this.destroyRef).

prompt: Which flattening operator should you use for a typeahead search box?
explanation: switchMap cancels the previous in-flight request when a new term arrives, so a stale response can't overwrite a newer one.

prompt: Match each combination operator to its behavior.

pairs.right: Emit latest of each when any source emits
Wait for all sources to complete, then emit once
Emit on the primary stream, adding the latest of a secondary

explanation: Each combines independent streams differently; picking the right one expresses the intended data dependency.

prompt: Where should catchError usually be placed relative to a flattening operator, and why?

options.text: After the flattening operator, to catch everything at once
Inside the flattening operator's callback, so an inner failure doesn't terminate the whole outer stream
Before the flattening operator, on the source
It doesn't matter where it goes

explanation: Placing catchError after the operator lets an inner error kill the outer stream permanently; inside it catches only that inner failure.

prompt: When would you choose exhaustMap over switchMap?

options.text: For a live search where only the latest input matters
To ignore new triggers while an operation is in flight, e.g. preventing duplicate form submits
To run all requests in parallel

explanation: exhaustMap ignores new source values until the current inner Observable completes — ideal for a Save button.

prompt: Why prefer shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }) over shareReplay(1)?

options.text: refCount: true tears down the source subscription when there are no subscribers, avoiding a memory leak

explanation: The bare shareReplay(1) shorthand keeps the source alive forever; refCount cleans up when unused.

prompt: Which @angular/core/rxjs-interop operator auto-completes a manual subscription when the component is destroyed?
explanation: takeUntilDestroyed() replaces the manual Subject + takeUntil + ngOnDestroy cleanup boilerplate.

prompt: Which operator emits a value, then ignores further values for a fixed window, even while events keep arriving?
explanation: throttleTime rate-limits while events continue. debounceTime instead waits for a pause before emitting.

prompt: A switchMap branch for an empty search term returns EMPTY. What does an async pipe on the result show?

options.text: The previous results stay, because EMPTY emits no value

explanation: EMPTY completes without emitting. To clear the list, return of([]) so a value is emitted.

prompt: What happens when you read a toSignal() signal whose source Observable has errored?

options.text: Reading the signal throws that error

explanation: toSignal surfaces the error when read. Put catchError inside the pipeline so one failure does not make the signal unreadable.

prompt: Which sequence does the Observable contract allow?
explanation: Any number of next, then at most one error or complete. Nothing is delivered after the stream has ended.

prompt: A search uses mergeMap and sometimes shows results for an older term. Why?

options.text: mergeMap does not cancel earlier requests, so a slow old response can arrive last

explanation: mergeMap runs inner requests concurrently with no cancellation. Use switchMap so only the latest request's response counts.

prompt: What is the difference between an action and a reducer in NgRx?

options.text: An action mutates state; a reducer describes an event
An action is a plain object describing that something happened; a reducer is a pure function computing new state from state + action

explanation: Actions carry intent with no logic; reducers purely derive the next state, never mutating the existing state.

prompt: Match each NgRx building block to its responsibility.

pairs.right: Performs side effects like HTTP and dispatches results

explanation: These four pieces implement the unidirectional Redux data flow that makes state changes traceable.

prompt: Where should HTTP/API calls happen in an NgRx app?

options.text: Inside effects, which then dispatch success/failure actions

explanation: Isolating side effects in effects keeps reducers pure and preserves the traceable action-to-API narrative.

prompt: When should you choose a signalStore (@ngrx/signals) over the global Store?

options.text: For state shared across many unrelated features
For state local to one component or small feature (filters, pagination, UI flags)
Never — always use the global Store

explanation: A signalStore keeps local or feature state immutable and signal-based without adding global actions and reducers.

prompt: How do you scope a signalStore to a single component instance?

options.text: Add it to that component's own providers array

explanation: Providing it in the component's providers ties its lifecycle to that instance; { providedIn: 'root' } would make it an app-wide singleton.

prompt: Which @ngrx/operators helper safely handles success/error inside an effect or rxMethod so an error doesn't terminate the outer stream?
explanation: A plain catchError that rethrows can kill the effect; tapResponse separates next/error handling safely.

prompt: Match each SignalStore feature to its job.

pairs.right: Adds state properties, each exposed as a signal
Adds read-only signals derived from the state
Updates state immutably from inside a method

explanation: State, derived values, and methods are added as features; only the store's own methods change state, through patchState.

prompt: What is the preferred way to read a NgRx selector into a component template?

options.text: Read store state directly with an inline arrow function

explanation: selectSignal returns a signal with no subscription to manage, and keeps reading through a named, memoized selector.

prompt: A state has the property isLoading. What selector does createFeature generate for it?
explanation: createFeature derives selector names from the property names: isLoading becomes selectIsLoading.

prompt: Which action name best follows the 'event, not command' guidance?
explanation: Events describe what happened and who did it, so several reducers and effects can react independently.

prompt: A reducer does state.count++ and returns state. What goes wrong?

options.text: The object reference is unchanged, so selectors and OnPush views see no change
Nothing; mutation is allowed in reducers

explanation: Mutation keeps the same reference, so reference comparisons skip the update, and DevTools history becomes wrong. Return a new object.

prompt: What does ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush tell Angular to do?

options.text: Never run change detection on the component
Skip checking the component's view unless a specific trigger occurs
Check the component twice per cycle

explanation: OnPush prunes checks to only when there's a trackable reason — it doesn't disable change detection entirely.

prompt: Why does mutating an object passed via @Input() fail to update an OnPush component?

options.text: Angular does a deep structural comparison that's too slow
Angular compares inputs by reference, so mutating in place leaves the reference unchanged
Objects cannot be used as inputs

explanation: Reference (Object.is) comparison means you must produce a new object/array for OnPush to detect the change.

prompt: Which of the following trigger a check on an OnPush component? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: An event fires within the component or its children
An async pipe in the template emits a new value
A signal read in the template changes

explanation: New input reference, an internal event, an async pipe emission, a markForCheck() call, or a changed signal all trigger a check.

prompt: What is the difference between markForCheck() and detectChanges()?

options.text: markForCheck() schedules a check for the next cycle; detectChanges() runs one immediately and synchronously

explanation: Prefer markForCheck() (safe, scheduled) unless you specifically need the immediate synchronous run of detectChanges().

prompt: Do signals require OnPush or Zone.js to update the UI?

options.text: No — reading a signal in a template registers it as a dependency, so Angular schedules a targeted update independent of Zone.js
Signals cannot update the UI at all

explanation: Signals wire fine-grained updates automatically, which is why OnPush + Signals is the on-ramp to zoneless Angular.

prompt: The async pipe works seamlessly under OnPush because it internally calls which ChangeDetectorRef method on every emission?
explanation: The async pipe calls markForCheck() for you, so observable data 'just works' with OnPush.

prompt: Since Angular 22, which change detection strategy do components use if they don't set one?

options.text: Zone-based checking of the whole tree

explanation: Since Angular 22, OnPush is the default and the old behavior is called ChangeDetectionStrategy.Eager (Default is deprecated). On Angular 20 and 21 you opt in to OnPush per component.

prompt: What problem do Web Workers solve in an Angular app?

options.text: They make pipes re-run less often
They move CPU-intensive work off the main thread so the UI stays responsive
They give components access to a second DOM

explanation: Workers run on a separate thread, so long computations don't freeze rendering, animations, or input on the main thread.

prompt: How do the main thread and a worker exchange data?

options.text: Through message passing (postMessage/onmessage); data is copied via structured clone

explanation: Workers are isolated — they communicate only by copied (or transferred) messages, never shared references.

prompt: When does a pure pipe's transform() method re-run?

options.text: Only when a primitive input changes value, or an object/array input changes by reference
Only once, when the component is created
Whenever any signal in the app changes

explanation: Pure pipes memoize by reference/value equality and reuse the cached output otherwise.

prompt: Why doesn't a pure pipe re-run after array.push(item)?

options.text: push() mutates in place, so the array reference stays the same and the pipe sees no change

explanation: Create a new reference instead, e.g. items.set([...items(), item]), so the reference-equality check detects the change.

prompt: What must you always do with a worker you no longer need?

options.text: Call worker.terminate() (on completion, on error, and on destroy)

explanation: An un-terminated worker keeps running in the background; use DestroyRef.onDestroy() as a safety net too.

prompt: Which signal API offers the same lazy, memoized derivation as a pure pipe but works anywhere in TypeScript, not just templates?
explanation: computed() recomputes only when a dependency changes and caches its result, usable throughout component logic.

prompt: What does virtual scrolling do?

options.text: Renders every list item but hides the off-screen ones with CSS
Renders only the DOM elements currently visible (plus a small buffer), recycling nodes as you scroll
Loads the whole list from the server at once

explanation: Only the visible window of items is in the DOM, so a 100,000-row list scrolls like a 20-row one.

prompt: Why must a cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport have an explicit height in CSS?

options.text: The CDK computes the visible item range from the viewport's dimensions and scroll offset; without a bounded height there's nothing to scroll

explanation: A bounded height (plus itemSize) lets the FixedSizeVirtualScrollStrategy calculate which rows to render.

prompt: After a drag, who is responsible for updating your underlying data array?

options.text: The CDK updates the data automatically
You are — in the (cdkDropListDropped) handler, using moveItemInArray or transferArrayItem

explanation: The CDK only moves the visual representation; you own the data and call the helper functions in the drop handler.

prompt: Match each drag/drop helper or directive to its role.

pairs.right: Move an item between two lists' arrays
Restrict the grabbable area to a child element

explanation: These building blocks compose into reorderable and Kanban-style interfaces.

prompt: You use moveItemInArray on a signal-backed array under OnPush, but the UI doesn't update. Why?

options.text: The helper mutates the array in place, so you must replace the reference (e.g. signal.update(a => [...a]))

explanation: moveItemInArray/transferArrayItem mutate by reference; produce a new reference or call markForCheck() so change detection picks it up.

prompt: For fixed-size virtual scrolling, which viewport attribute must match the real pixel height of one row?
explanation: A mismatched itemSize is the #1 cause of janky/jumpy virtual scrolling.

prompt: How should keyboard users reorder items in a list built with CDK drag and drop?

options.text: Focus the drag handle and press Space and the arrow keys; the CDK handles it
Provide another control, such as Move up / Move down buttons, that calls the same reorder logic
They cannot, and nothing needs to be done
Add tabindex="0" to every cdkDrag element

explanation: CDK drag and drop is pointer- and touch-based. Give keyboard users buttons or a menu that call moveItemInArray(), and announce the change with LiveAnnouncer.

prompt: Match each page to the render mode that suits it best.

pairs.left: A blog post that is the same for everyone
A product page with live prices

explanation: Prerender what is identical for everyone, server-render public dynamic pages, and client-render private pages.

prompt: What is hydration?

options.text: Downloading data before the app starts
The browser-side app reusing the server-rendered DOM instead of rebuilding it
Compressing the HTML on the server
